title: Python: foundations to advanced

topics.title: Variables & expressions
topics.lesson:
Python executes statements in order. A variable is a name bound to a value: price = 12 binds price to an integer. Reassigning price changes that binding; it does not rewrite earlier calculations. Names are case-sensitive. Use descriptive snake_case names and never begin a name with a digit.

Integers represent whole numbers; floats represent approximate fractional numbers. The operators +, -, *, /, //, %, and ** mean addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, remainder, and exponentiation. Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. Multiplication binds more tightly than addition. / returns a float, while // rounds the quotient down, including for negatives.

A string contains text in quotes. An expression such as 3 + 4 produces a value; an assignment stores a value under a name. print displays a value, whereas return sends a value back from a function. In the coding exercises a solve function is provided: put your calculation after return. Functions are taught in depth later.
topics.pitfall: Use == to compare and = to assign. Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero.
topics.example:
price = 12
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print(total)
print(17 // 5, 17 % 5)

topics.title: Types & conversion
topics.lesson:
Python values have types; names do not have permanently declared types. int, float, str, bool and None are common built-in value categories. type(value) inspects a type and isinstance(value, int) checks membership in a type. bool is a subclass of int, so distinguish the two deliberately when validating input.

Convert explicitly with int, float and str. int("12") succeeds, while int("12.5") raises ValueError. int(12.9) truncates toward zero. float("12.5") produces 12.5. input() always returns text; convert it before doing arithmetic. This platform supplies function arguments directly, so submitted solutions normally do not use input().

Empty strings, zero, None and empty containers are false in a condition. Nonempty strings are true, including "False". None represents absence, not the text "None". Compare None with is None. Floating-point arithmetic is approximate; round for presentation and avoid assuming arbitrary decimal fractions are exact.
topics.pitfall: bool("False") is True because the string is nonempty. int cannot directly parse a decimal-point string.
topics.example:
raw = "24"
count = int(raw)
print(count + 1)
print(bool(""), bool("False"))

topics.title: Conditions & logic
topics.lesson:
An if statement executes its indented body only when its condition is true. elif checks an alternative only if earlier branches were false; else covers the remaining cases. Use four spaces per indentation level. A chain of separate if statements can execute several bodies; an if/elif chain selects at most one.

Comparisons include ==, !=, <, <=, > and >=. Python supports chained comparisons: 0 <= score <= 100. and requires both conditions to hold; or requires at least one. not reverses truth. These operators short-circuit: the right side may not be evaluated. This makes checks such as denominator != 0 and numerator / denominator > 2 possible.

Order specific conditions before general ones. For grading, test the highest threshold first. For a compound classification, test the combined case before either individual case. Think through boundaries and equality, not just typical inputs. A conditional expression, a if condition else b, selects a value in one expression.
topics.pitfall: Indentation defines the block. Put the combined divisibility case before either individual case.

topics.title: Loops & iteration
topics.lesson:
A for loop visits each item of an iterable. range(stop) generates integers from zero up to, but not including, stop. range(start, stop, step) changes the start and step; a negative step counts down. range is not a list, but it can be iterated without materialising all its numbers.

A while loop repeats while its condition stays true. Ensure its body changes something that can make the condition false. break exits the nearest loop; continue skips to its next iteration. The optional loop else block runs only if the loop finishes without break, which is useful for searches.

An accumulator starts from a neutral value, such as zero for a sum or an empty list for collected results. Update it once per relevant item. For nested loops, trace the inner loop fully for each outer iteration. Two loops of length n nested together usually perform n squared iterations; a single pass is often preferable. Trace small inputs on paper to find off-by-one errors.
topics.pitfall: range excludes its stop. Do not change a list’s size while iterating over it unless the behaviour is deliberate.
topics.example:
total = 0
for number in range(1, 6):
    total += number
print(total)

topics.title: Strings & text
topics.lesson:
Strings are immutable sequences of Unicode characters. Index zero selects the first character; negative indices count from the end. A slice text[start:stop:step] excludes stop. Slices tolerate endpoints outside the string, while a single invalid index raises IndexError.

Methods such as lower, upper, strip and replace return new strings. split separates text into a list; separator.join(parts) assembles strings. With no separator, split treats runs of whitespace as a single separator. f-strings insert values into text: f"Hello {name}". Escape sequences such as \n represent special characters.

Define normalisation before comparing text. A case-insensitive palindrome exercise may ignore spaces, while another may ignore all punctuation; those are different requirements. isalnum and isalpha understand Unicode, not only English letters. Repeated concatenation in a loop can be wasteful; collecting pieces and joining them is clearer for larger outputs.
topics.pitfall: Calling text.upper() does not change text unless you assign the returned string.
topics.example:
text = "  Python path  "
print(text.strip().upper())
print("-".join(text.split()))

topics.title: Lists & tuples
topics.lesson:
Lists are ordered mutable sequences. append adds one object, extend adds each item from an iterable, and pop removes and returns an item. Slicing creates a shallow copy: the outer list is new but nested objects may still be shared. Assigning b = a creates another reference to the same list.

Tuples are ordered and immutable at the container level. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (3,). A tuple can contain mutable objects, so immutable does not mean every nested value is immutable. Unpacking assigns sequence items to several names; a starred target collects the remainder.

sorted(values) returns a new sorted list; values.sort() sorts a list in place and returns None. min, max and sum handle common reductions, but min and max need a nonempty iterable unless a default is supplied. Specify how empty input should behave. For list transformations, decide whether preserving the input is part of the contract.
topics.pitfall: list.sort() returns None. [[0] * 3] * 2 shares its inner list; use a comprehension for independent rows.
topics.example:
values = [3, 1, 2]
copy = sorted(values)
print(values, copy)
first, *rest = copy
print(first, rest)

topics.title: Dictionaries & sets
topics.lesson:
A dictionary maps unique hashable keys to values. Use mapping[key] when a missing key is an error, or mapping.get(key, default) when a default makes sense. Assigning an existing key replaces its value. Modern Python dictionaries preserve insertion order; that is not automatic alphabetical sorting.

A set contains unique hashable elements and does not promise a useful iteration order. Use set() for an empty set; {} creates an empty dictionary. Set union, intersection and difference are written a | b, a & b and a - b. Dictionary keys and set elements must be hashable, so a list cannot be a key.

Frequency counting is a common dictionary pattern: counts[x] = counts.get(x, 0) + 1. Iterate .items() for key/value pairs. Membership in a dictionary checks keys. When returning set-derived results in an exercise, sort them if deterministic order is required. A shallow dictionary copy still shares nested objects.
topics.pitfall: {} is a dictionary. Membership in a dictionary tests keys, not values.

topics.title: Functions & scope
topics.lesson:
def creates a function with parameters and a body. Calling it binds arguments to parameters and executes that body. return ends the call and provides a result; reaching the end without return yields None. Printing is a side effect, not a substitute for returning a result.

Positional arguments match by order; keyword arguments match by parameter name. Defaults are evaluated once when the function is defined. Use None as a default for an optional fresh list, then create the list inside the call. *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keywords into a dictionary.

Python resolves names through local, enclosing, global and built-in scopes. Assignment inside a function usually makes a name local. Prefer explicit inputs and returned results to hidden global state. Functions are values: they can be passed to other functions. A docstring states the contract, while type hints communicate intended types without automatically enforcing them at runtime.
topics.pitfall: Default mutable arguments are shared across calls. Prefer None and initialise inside the function.
topics.example:
def greet(name, prefix="Hello"):
    return f"{prefix}, {name}"
print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Ada", prefix="Welcome"))

topics.title: Comprehensions
topics.lesson:
A list comprehension builds a list from an iterable: [expression for item in items]. An optional if filters which items contribute. Filtering is different from an if/else expression that chooses the output value. Comprehensions can be clearer than a loop when the transformation is short and free of side effects.

Set comprehensions use braces around values; dictionary comprehensions use key: value pairs. A generator expression uses parentheses and produces values lazily. Avoid building an entire list when you only need to sum it. Nested comprehensions follow the same loop order as equivalent nested for statements.

Choose readability over cleverness. If a transformation needs several statements, error handling or complex branching, use an explicit loop or helper function. Comprehensions have their own iteration-variable scope in Python 3. A new outer container does not necessarily deep-copy its elements.
topics.pitfall: Place a filter after the for clause; place a value-selecting if/else before it.
topics.example:
numbers = range(6)
print([n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0])
print({n: n * n for n in range(3)})

topics.title: Exceptions & validation
topics.lesson:
Exceptions signal that an operation could not complete normally. try surrounds the risky operation; except handles specific failures. Catch the narrowest useful exception, such as ValueError for invalid conversion or ZeroDivisionError for division by zero. Catching every exception can hide programming mistakes.

else runs when the try body succeeds. finally runs during normal completion and exception unwinding and is useful for cleanup. raise creates or propagates an exception. Validate a function’s contract explicitly when invalid inputs must be rejected. Assertions are development checks, not a replacement for user input validation because Python can disable them.

Separate a failure from a valid result: None can represent missing data if documented, while zero might be a legitimate answer. Preserve useful error messages. Inside an except block, bare raise propagates the current exception. Use resource context managers rather than manually repeating cleanup code.
topics.pitfall: Do not catch Exception and silently return a success value; that hides unrelated bugs.

topics.title: Files & JSON
topics.lesson:
open creates a file object. Use with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle so the file closes even if reading raises an exception. Mode r reads, w replaces existing content, and a appends. Text mode works with strings; binary mode works with bytes. Paths refer to the machine or runtime executing Python.

Read a small file with read(), or iterate over lines for larger files. strip removes whitespace, so use it only when whitespace is not meaningful. JSON represents null, booleans, numbers, strings, arrays and string-keyed objects. json.loads parses a string; json.dumps serialises a compatible Python value. JSON cannot directly represent arbitrary Python objects or sets.

Browser Python has a virtual filesystem: it cannot silently read your Desktop files. Our exercises use supplied text or in-memory streams for portability. Validate the structure after parsing JSON: syntactically valid JSON may still have the wrong fields or types. Never use eval to parse untrusted data.
topics.pitfall: Opening with w truncates a file. JSON uses double quotes and is not arbitrary Python source.
topics.example:
import json
from io import StringIO
with StringIO("first\nsecond\n") as handle:
    print([line.strip() for line in handle])
print(json.loads('{"score": 8}')["score"])

topics.title: Modules & standard library
topics.lesson:
A module is a Python file or importable unit. import math binds the module name; math.sqrt then accesses an attribute. from math import sqrt binds that attribute directly. Avoid wildcard imports because they obscure where names come from. Do not name your own file math.py or json.py when you intend to import the standard module.

A package organises modules under a shared namespace. A virtual environment separates third-party dependencies between projects. The standard library is distributed with Python and includes math, statistics, collections, itertools and pathlib. Third-party packages require installation and may not support browser Python.

Top-level module code executes on first import in a process. The guard if __name__ == "__main__": keeps command-line behaviour separate from reusable functions. Keep imports near the start of a module, avoid circular dependencies and expose small, clear APIs. Use deterministic standard-library utilities instead of rewriting well-tested common operations.
topics.pitfall: A file named random.py can shadow the standard library module. Browser runtimes do not support every desktop package.
topics.example:
import math
from collections import Counter
print(math.gcd(12, 18))
print(Counter("banana"))

topics.title: Classes & objects
topics.lesson:
A class defines behaviour and structure for instances. __init__ initialises a newly created instance; self refers to the instance receiving a method call. Store per-instance state on self, such as self.balance. Class attributes belong to the class and can be shared; a mutable class attribute is usually wrong for independent per-object lists.

Methods are functions accessed through an object. A property can expose computed data through attribute syntax. __repr__ provides a developer-oriented representation. A dataclass can generate routine initialisation and representation methods, but does not automatically validate values.

Encapsulation means offering meaningful operations that preserve an object’s rules. A counter with increment and value operations can be clearer than scattered arithmetic on globals. Prefer a plain function when there is no persistent state or meaningful object relationship. Test several independent instances to catch accidental shared state.
topics.pitfall: Create each instance’s mutable state inside __init__, not as a shared class list.

topics.title: Inheritance & composition
topics.lesson:
Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a subclass can reuse and specialise a base class. Overriding replaces a method for that subclass. super() delegates according to the method resolution order; it is preferable to hard-coding a parent name in cooperative hierarchies.

Polymorphism means callers can use a common operation across different object types. Python often relies on duck typing: if an object supports the needed operation, it can be used without an explicit common base. Composition models a has-a relationship by storing one object inside another and delegating work.

Use inheritance when substitutability makes sense. A subclass should preserve the base operation’s expectations. Choose composition for assembling interchangeable components. Deep inheritance chains complicate reasoning; a small hierarchy or a set of functions is often enough. __str__ and other special methods support Python protocols, not arbitrary magic naming.
topics.pitfall: Inheritance should preserve the base interface’s meaning. Composition is often clearer for optional capabilities.

topics.title: Recursion & algorithms
topics.lesson:
A recursive function solves a problem using smaller instances of the same problem. It needs a base case that returns directly and a recursive step that moves toward that base case. Without either, recursion can continue until Python raises RecursionError. Each call has its own local state.

Trace a small input through both the descent and the return. Recursive factorial multiplies n by factorial(n-1), with factorial(0)=1. Repeated subproblems can make naive recursion expensive; memoisation caches results. Python does not generally eliminate tail calls, so a loop is safer for very deep sequences.

Algorithm choice matters more than clever syntax. Linear search examines items in order; binary search requires sorted data and repeatedly halves the remaining interval. Describe the input contract and edge cases. Our recursion exercises use small inputs; passing output tests alone does not prove the requested technique was used.
topics.pitfall: Every recursive branch must approach a base case. Do not use deep recursion for arbitrarily large inputs.

topics.title: Iterators & generators
topics.lesson:
An iterable can provide an iterator through iter(). An iterator supplies successive values through next() and signals exhaustion with StopIteration. A list can create new iterators repeatedly; an iterator itself remembers its position and is normally consumed once.

A function containing yield is a generator function. Calling it creates a generator; execution starts when a value is requested. yield pauses the function and preserves local state for the next request. return ends the generator. Generator expressions provide a compact lazy form for simple transformations.

Laziness is useful for pipelines and large or unbounded sequences, but it changes when work and errors happen. list(generator) materialises all remaining values and defeats memory savings for large streams. itertools.islice can take a finite prefix without consuming everything. Do not try to turn an infinite generator into a list.
topics.pitfall: A consumed generator does not restart; create a new generator for another traversal.

topics.title: Closures & decorators
topics.lesson:
A closure is a function that retains access to names from an enclosing function after that outer call has returned. It can capture configuration such as a multiplier. nonlocal allows reassignment of an enclosing function variable; reading it does not require nonlocal.

A decorator receives a callable and returns a callable, commonly a wrapper that adds behaviour before or after the original call. @decorate above a function is equivalent to rebinding that function to decorate(function). Forward *args and **kwargs so the wrapper preserves calling flexibility.

functools.wraps copies useful metadata such as the original name and docstring and exposes __wrapped__. Decorators can validate, log or cache, but should preserve the wrapped function’s contract unless explicitly documented. Capturing a changing loop variable can surprise you because closures look up the binding when called; capture a current value explicitly when needed.
topics.pitfall: A wrapper must return the original result when preserving behaviour. Use functools.wraps for metadata.

topics.title: Context managers
topics.lesson:
A context manager defines setup and cleanup around a with block. __enter__ runs at entry and its return value can be bound after as. __exit__ runs when the block finishes, including when an exception propagates. It receives exception information; returning a truthy value suppresses that exception, which should be deliberate.

contextlib.contextmanager lets a generator function define a context manager with one yield. Place cleanup in finally so it runs when the body fails. The value yielded becomes the as target. Use this pattern for resources, temporary state or instrumentation.

Files are the familiar example, but the same protocol works with locks and transactions. A context manager’s cleanup is about resource lifecycle, not proving the work succeeded. In browser exercises we use in-memory streams or event lists so no access to local files is needed.
topics.pitfall: Returning True from __exit__ suppresses an exception. Do not do it accidentally.
topics.example:
from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def tracked():
    print("enter")
    try: yield
    finally: print("exit")
with tracked():
    print("work")

topics.title: Testing & debugging
topics.lesson:
A test compares observed behaviour with an expected result. Unit tests target a small function or object; integration tests check components together. Choose normal cases, boundaries, empty inputs and invalid inputs according to the contract. A test that merely repeats the implementation may reproduce the same bug.

Arrange inputs, act by calling the function, and assert the result. unittest is in the standard library; pytest is a third-party alternative. Regression tests preserve a fixed bug’s behaviour. Test names should state what matters. For floating-point outputs, use an appropriate tolerance rather than exact equality when the contract permits approximation.

Debugging starts with a reproducible failing example. Read the traceback from the final exception to relevant call frames, inspect values, and reduce the problem. Passing a finite set of tests does not prove all possible inputs work. Our coding tests check outputs; technique requirements such as recursion or inheritance still benefit from code review.
topics.pitfall: Write expected results independently. Do not silently catch a failing assertion and report success.
topics.example:
import unittest
def add(a, b): return a + b
class AddTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_negative(self):
        self.assertEqual(add(-2, 3), 1)
suite = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(AddTests)
unittest.TextTestRunner().run(suite)

topics.title: Async & concurrency
topics.lesson:
async def defines a coroutine function. Calling it creates a coroutine object; await drives it within an event loop. asyncio.run starts and closes an event loop for a synchronous entry point. An event loop cooperatively switches tasks when they await operations that yield control.

Concurrency is overlapping progress; parallelism is simultaneous execution. Async I/O helps when waiting dominates, such as network requests. It does not automatically speed up CPU-bound Python calculations. Blocking calls such as time.sleep block the event loop; use await asyncio.sleep in asynchronous code.

asyncio.gather schedules awaitables and returns results in input order, not completion order. Handle failures and cancellation deliberately and clean up resources. Do not call asyncio.run inside an already running event loop. Our exercise runner executes synchronous solve wrappers; use asyncio.run there. For real applications, use async entry points consistently and apply timeouts to external operations.
topics.pitfall: Calling an async function without awaiting or scheduling it does not run its body to completion.
topics.example:
import asyncio
async def work(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return x * 2
async def main():
    return await asyncio.gather(work(2), work(3))
print(asyncio.run(main()))

activities.title: Prime check
activities.prompt: Return whether integer n is prime. Integers below 2 are not prime.
activities.solution:
def solve(n):
    if n < 2: return False
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0: return False
        d += 1
    return True

activities.title: Gather squares
activities.prompt: Compute squares in coroutines with gather; return results in the input order.
activities.solution:
def solve(values):
    import asyncio
    async def square(x):
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return x * x
    async def main(): return await asyncio.gather(*(square(x) for x in values))
    return asyncio.run(main())

activities.title: Collect success or failure

activities.solution:
def solve(values):
    import asyncio
    async def work(x): return 10 // x
    async def main():
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(work(x) for x in values), return_exceptions=True)
        return [None if isinstance(x, Exception) else x for x in results]
    return asyncio.run(main())
